sources.citation: Man, Edward Horace. 1889. A dictionary of the Central Nicobarese language. London: W.H. Allen. (archive.org id adictionarycent00mangoog, djvu text)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Stress rules in the orthography notes ('In disyllabic words stress occurs on the second syllable unless there is a long vowel in the first syllable.. In trisyllabic and polysyllabic words stress usually occurs on the penultimate syllable..') are for Central Nicobarese (Nancowry), not Shom Pen. Introduction (djvu lines 626-629, page number not recoverable from scanned): 'Unlike Chinese and Burmese, no instance has been discovered in any of the dialects in which the meaning of words depends on tone, accent, or emphasis' - a blanket Nicobarese-dialects remark; Shom Pen appears only as comparativ…

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Shompen language' (accessed 2026-09-17); WALS entry smp Shompen (source Chattopadhyay-and-Mukhopadhyay-2003); Glottolog 5.1 shom1245 page (family membership per Blench 2007)
sources.access_detail: read online, no copy kept
sources.note: Wikipedia's phonology section (8 vowel qualities recovered by Blench & Sidwell, nasalisation/length, consonant chart, sound changes) says nothing about stress or tone; WALS and Glottolog give bibliography only. Glottolog's 9 'descriptive' refs for shom1245 are all mis-linked (Romance/morphology proceedings, W. Jones 1798) and were disregarded.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger & Paul Sidwell. 2011. Is Shom Pen a distinct branch of Austroasiatic? In S. Srichampa & P. Sidwell (eds), Austroasiatic Studies: papers from ICAAL4 (Mon-Khmer Studies Journal Special Issue No. 3 / Pacific Linguistics E-9), 9-18.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No stress statement. §3 reinterprets C&M 2003's transcription (their ā = schwa; double vowels = length; 'in' = ɲ). The only use of 'unstressed' is p. 11, point 3: in Malay loans and Nicobarese/Aslian cognates C&M's /ā/ corresponds to /ə, ɨ, ɯ/ or unstressed /a/ - a remark about the cognate languages, not about Shom Pen stress.

sources.citation: Schiering, René & Harry van der Hulst. 2010. Word accent systems in the languages of Asia. In Goedemans, van der Hulst & van Zanten (eds), A survey of word accentual patterns in the languages of the world, 509-599. De Gruyter Mouton.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: publisher record (DOI); no open copy and no library e-access found (also a publisher record (DOI), probably paywalled)
sources.note: Shom Peng appears only as a name in the Austroasiatic language list (p. 591, 'SHOM PENG: Shom Peng'); no StressTyp entry or data.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2007. The language of the Shom Pen: a language isolate in the Nicobar islands. Draft circulated for comment, Cambridge, 21 Sept 2007, 22 pp. (§3 Shom Pen phonology; §4 annotated wordlist)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. §3 covers only vowels (7 phonemic, all nasalisable, only /a/ with a long counterpart ā), consonants and orthographic conversions, all summarised second-hand from Chattopadhyay & Mukhopadhyay 2003; no occurrence of stress/accent/tone/prosody in the whole text (a full-text search for stress/accent full text).

sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: The only primary description; contains a Phonology chapter (Google Books table of contents) and is the sole data source behind every later phonological remark (Blench 2007; Blench & Sidwell 2011). Any first-hand statement on Shompen stress/syllable prominence would be here (Blench & Sidwell caution that its transcription is unreliable, e.g. ā likely = schwa).
